description: DETON8 is taking part in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge with the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. We are software engineers and data scientists, coming from LLM pipelines with RAG to computer vision and real-time applications, here to apply that experience to human exploration and to show that a team from the northeast of Brazil can help shape how humanity will explore other worlds.
summary:
H2G2 (Human-to-Ground Guide) is a hyperlocal field guide for a safe astronaut walk on Mars, set in the boxwork of Mount Sharp, Gale Crater, the example named in the challenge. Global maps like Mars Trek show regions; an astronaut needs meters.

We built a layered map covering ~3x3 km at walking scale, combining data from several missions: HiRISE, CTX, THEMIS thermal inertia, CRISM, and Curiosity's REMS, RAD, ChemCam, APXS and CheMin. On top of it: A* routes with explained risk (slope, radiation dose, estimated O2 per segment), slope risk calibrated against 293 Curiosity stops, hour-by-hour sun and shadow, 211 photos and 73 panoramas placed on the map, science cards for 10 real targets, an offline weather forecast with measured error, and Marvin, a local voice assistant.

Three principles make it realistic. It runs fully offline, because Mars has no internet and Earth is 4-24 minutes away. It never invents: with no data, it says so. Every fact shows its source and confidence level.

It matters because the first crews will decide in the field, without waiting for Earth. H2G2 gives them map, route, science and conditions at the scale of their boots, all from open NASA data.
details:
What it does

H2G2 (Human-to-Ground Guide) is a hyperlocal field guide for an astronaut walking on Mars. It covers ~3x3 km of the boxwork on Mount Sharp, Gale Crater, centered on Curiosity's real position during its 2025 campaign. Mars Trek and USGS geologic maps show global and regional views; H2G2 works at the scale of a walk.

How it works

- Layered map: HiRISE (~0.6 m/px), CTX, HiRISE DTM hillshade, THEMIS thermal inertia, slope risk, sun and shadow, and REMS/RAD conditions along the traverse, plus 13 official IAU/USGS names.

- Routes with explained risk: A* over real terrain with three variants (safest, fastest, most science) and optional waypoints. Slope caution at 15° and danger above 20° (Artemis walking limit), radiation dose from RAD summed over the walk, and O2 estimated per segment as an optimistic-pessimistic range (350 W base rate from NASA ICES-2026-158, slope effect from the Pandolf equation as used by NASA/JSC). If the astronaut reports a problem (rock, slope, fatigue, dust, O2), the system replans and the astronaut chooses. Risk labels come from fixed rules, never from the LLM, and no route is hidden.

- Slope risk calibrated by the rover: orbital terrain smooths 1-2 m ridges. We compared the map with slopes Curiosity measured at 293 stops. Where the map says 10-15°, 27% of stops measured 15° or more; where it says 15° or more, 80% did (n = 5). This becomes a "chance the ground exceeds 15°" per point and segment. It is a historical frequency, not a prediction.

- Sun and shadow by the hour: direct solar irradiance per pixel for any sol and local time, using our implementation of the Mars24 algorithm, the HiRISE DTM (computed at 2 m) and the MOLA horizon to include Mount Sharp's shadow. It is an upper bound (no dust or diffuse light).

- Photos and panoramas: 211 Navcam photos and 73 360° panoramas placed by rover stop. The interface says "taken X m from here".

- Science cards: 10 boxwork targets with 60 real PDS measurements (ChemCam, APXS, CheMin), plus CRISM orbital context, Mastcam photo and confidence on every line.

- Conditions and offline forecast: REMS and RAD measurements, plus a seasonal climatology built from 231 REMS sols across the mission, corrected by the latest measured anomaly. Backtested 20 sols ahead (n = 201): mean error 1.9 °C for minimum temperature, 3.7 °C for maximum, 11.2 Pa for pressure. It also suggests the best time window for the EVA and warns when a day is out of the seasonal norm.

- Marvin, an offline voice assistant: "Hey Marvin" or push-to-talk, local Whisper speech recognition and a local LLM (gemma4 via Ollama). Emergencies (fall, leak, toxic gas) are handled by fixed rules with an immediate response, and cited sources come from the system, not from the model's text.

Benefits and intended impact

The first crews will make decisions in the field, without waiting 4-24 minutes for Earth. H2G2 gives them map, route, science and conditions at the scale of their boots, and tells them how much to trust each number. It also shows how open NASA data from several missions can be fused into an operational tool.

Tools

Python, FastAPI and SQLite (native R-tree) on the backend; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules, no framework) on the front end, with vendored MapLibre (map) and Pannellum (panoramas); Whisper and Ollama for local voice and language. All data is downloaded only at build time from NASA PDS, Mars Trek, USGS, MMGIS and the MSL raw image archive, then served from local files.

What makes it creative

- Rover-calibrated risk: Curiosity's own measurements correct what orbit cannot see.

- A guide that says "no data" instead of guessing.

- The Hitchhiker's Guide spirit: a pocket guide for surviving a strange place, with an assistant named Marvin and a "Don't Panic" motto.

Factors we considered

- Offline first: Mars has no internet, so maps, photos, measurements, voice and LLM all run locally. Our acceptance test: turn off Wi-Fi and use the whole system.

- Never invent: with no data, the system returns "no data" and says what is missing. Mock data exists only behind an explicit flag.

- Source and confidence on every line: instrument, PDS file and confidence come with every fact shown or spoken.

- Safety decisions by rule, not by AI.

- Gloved hands: voice is the main input. A helmet HUD is our proposed next step, shown as a 3D model.

- Small and realistic: few dependencies, data clipped to the area of interest.

- Honest limits: route risk runs on a ~6 m grid, sand is shown as a fixed warning, and the bundled conditions end at sol 4840 (the system shows how old the data is).
